editorial.headline: Certifying Your Own Talent: KBLI 85691
editorial.standfirst: A foreign-open activity for organisations assessing and certifying the professional competence of their own employees or students.
editorial.body:
Professional certification can be an important part of how an organisation recognises capability within its own ranks. This activity covers the assessment and certification of employees’ or students’ work and professional competencies by the organisation responsible for them. In the record’s terms, it is a first-party professional-certification activity: the focus is on measuring and certifying the competence of the organisation’s own people.

That scope gives the activity a clear institutional character. It speaks to an employer assessing its own workforce, or to an education and training organisation certifying its own students. The slim record does not specify any business scales open to this activity, so it does not support a claim that it is reserved for, or limited to, a particular size of organisation. What it does establish is the national PMA position: the activity is **TERBUKA**, with a maximum foreign ownership ceiling of 100%. Nationally, a foreign investor may therefore hold the full foreign-owned stake permitted for this activity.

Bali requires a more exact reading, but not a pessimistic one. The province applies an island-wide, permanent moratorium to PMA activities assessed as Low or Medium-Low risk. This activity is recorded instead as medium-high/high risk, and it is explicitly marked as not blocked by that moratorium. Bali is therefore open to PMA registration for this activity today, subject to verification for the specific address.

That distinction matters because the provincial result is not merely a restatement of the national position. National openness establishes the 100% foreign-ownership ceiling; Bali’s record addresses whether the provincial moratorium blocks registration. Here, it does not. A founder considering this activity in Bali should read the position plainly: the activity is foreign-open nationally, it is not barred by Bali’s Low and Medium-Low risk moratorium, and the address remains part of the verification required for the Bali registration picture.
